the splicing defect in this patient is caused by a substitution of the last base of exon 6, and that the splicing efficiency is temperature-dependent.

in the patient with the C-to-T transition in exon 6, the splicing defect was not temperature dependent, whereas in the patient with an inactivating mutation of the 5'-splice site of intron, the splicing was temperature dependent.

in the patient with Ehlers Danlos syndrome Type VII, the substitution in the last nucleotide (G-->T) of exon 6 causes an alternative splicing of pro-alpha 2(1) collagen mRNA, which is temperature-dependent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the molecular lesion in the patient with the substitution at the 3' splice site of the last nucleotides of exon 6 produces normally spliced and outspliced transcripts in a temperature-dependent fashion, whereas in the patient with a substitution of the 5 splice site of introns 6, only the latter is produced.
the temperature-dependent missplicing in the patient with the C to T mutation is due to the creation of a cryptic 3' splice site in the 3' end of exon 6.
the splicing defect of the pro-alpha2(I) collagen chain in EDS Type VII patients is caused by the substitution of the last G nucleotide of exon6, and this defect is temperature-dependent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single point mutation in a collagen gene can produce a variety of splicing defects, depending on its location and on the temperature at which the cells are grown.
the expression of a collagen gene splicing defect can be regulated by the temperature at which cells are maintained in culture.
